title: Opinion Writing — Writing Pack
summary: How to give and explain your view for full marks in Paper 1: opinion vs persuasive vs balanced argument, features, the REAP paragraph, useful phrases and a strong sample article.

blocks.text: **Opinion writing** gives your point of view on a topic and supports it with reasons, examples and evidence. Its aim is to make the reader **understand and agree with** what you think. An opinion task could ask for an article, a letter, an email, an essay or a speech. The format named in the task changes how you open and lay out your writing, but the thinking is the same.

blocks.title: Where it appears in the exam
items: Paper 1 Non-fiction, Section B Writing (25 marks, about 30 minutes suggested in a 1-hour paper).
Tasks may give a short situation, e.g. 'Your school magazine wants pupils' views on…', 'Write an article giving your opinion about…', 'Do you agree that…? Write a letter to…'.
Read the task carefully: if it asks for **both sides** fairly, that is a **balanced argument**. If it asks you to make someone **do** something, that is **persuasive writing**. Each has its own pack.

Its own paragraph method (see the persuasive pack)
To give and explain your opinion.
Often pupils, parents or teachers (school magazine, school website, class debate) or readers of a newspaper.
Formal or semi-formal, depending on the reader. Polite even when you disagree.
**First person** for your view (I believe…), **present tense** for the issue. 'We' and 'you' can bring readers in.

blocks.text: How your writing is marked (25 marks)

headers: What a top answer needs in opinion writing
rows: A clear opinion that stays the same from start to end, with well-developed reasons and examples. The tone suits the reader. All task bullets are covered.
Precise words that show strength of feeling (essential, valuable, harmful) and some persuasive tools chosen for effect.
Introduction with hook + background + opinion. One reason per paragraph. Linking words between paragraphs. A conclusion that restates the view.
Varied sentences (complex sentences with because, although, if), questions punctuated correctly, commas after openers.
Ambitious words spelt correctly, e.g. believe, opinion, necessary, concentrate, especially.

blocks.title: Marking rules you must know
items: 20 words or fewer scores 0. Between 21 and 60 words can score no more than 7 marks altogether.
If the task names a format (letter, article, speech), use it. Writing the wrong text type can cap Creation at 1 and Structure at 3 (or 2).
Changing your mind in the middle ('…but actually I think the opposite') makes your viewpoint unclear and loses Creation marks.

rows: The reader knows what you think from the start

Each point builds on the last

Article: title + subheadings. Letter: Dear…, Yours sincerely. Speech: Good morning, everyone.

blocks.text: An **essay** gives the opinion directly in the first paragraph (thesis statement). An **article** often starts in a more interesting way, with a short story, a fact or a question, and then gives the writer's opinion (the claim). An article can use subheadings, but an essay is written in paragraphs without them.

rows: Short and interesting. It can show your view
**Hook** (question, fact, mini-story) + **background** (what the issue is) + **your opinion** in one clear sentence
Have you ever fallen asleep with a book on your face? … I believe paper books are better.
Your strongest reason, with evidence, explanation and a persuasive tool
Paper books are better for our eyes.
Mention what others think, then show why your view is still stronger
Some say tablets are lighter. However, …
Restate your view in new words, sum up the reasons, end with a final thought, question or prediction
So next time you choose a story, reach for paper.

blocks.title: REAP: the method for each body paragraph
items: **R — Reason:** why you hold this opinion (the topic sentence).
**E — Evidence:** a fact, an example, a number or a short story from real life.
**A — Analysis:** explain how the evidence proves your reason (This shows that… This means that…).
**P — Persuasive tool:** finish with a rhetorical question, emotive language, the rule of three or a strong statement.

blocks.text: **REAP example:** *One important reason is that paper books help us concentrate.* (Reason) *When I read on a tablet, a message or a game notification often pops up after a few minutes.* (Evidence) *This means my attention jumps away from the story, and I have to read the same page again.* (Analysis) *How can we enjoy an adventure if we keep leaving it?* (Persuasive tool)
How to start: openings you can adapt

items: **A question:** Have you ever wondered why so many pupils feel tired on Monday mornings?
**A short story (anecdote):** Last summer, my little cousin jumped into the deep end of the pool, and for one terrible second, nobody moved.
**A surprising fact:** Children today spend more time looking at screens than playing outside. That worries me.
**Imagine…:** Imagine a school where every break time was spent in a beautiful green garden.
**Straight to the point (essay):** In my opinion, school uniforms are a good idea for three main reasons.

blocks.text: How to end: closings you can adapt

items: **Restate + final thought:** For all these reasons, I am convinced that every child should learn to swim. It is a skill that could one day save a life.
**A question to remember:** If something makes us healthier, happier and kinder, why would we not choose it?
**A prediction:** If we make this small change now, our school will be a better place for everyone next year.
**A gentle invitation:** Next time you have a choice, try it for yourself. I think you will agree with me.

blocks.title: Opinion article: paper books or screens?
blocks.task: Your school magazine is asking pupils: 'Is it better to read stories in paper books or on a screen?' Write an article giving your opinion. You should include: • your opinion • your reasons, with examples • what people who disagree might say.
text: Have you ever fallen asleep with a book on your face? I have, many times, and I always wake up smiling. These days, more and more pupils read stories on tablets and phones. Screens are useful, but when it comes to reading stories, I strongly believe that paper books are better.

One important reason is that paper books are kinder to our eyes. After an hour of reading on a tablet, my eyes often feel dry and sore, especially at night. With a paper book, I can read for much longer without a headache. This shows that paper lets us enjoy stories for longer. Surely our eyes deserve a rest from screens after a long school day?

Another reason is that paper books help us concentrate. When I read on a screen, a message or a game notification often pops up after a few minutes. My attention jumps away from the story, and I have to read the same page again. A book has no notifications, no adverts and no batteries. How can we enjoy an adventure if we keep leaving it?

Most importantly, paper books feel special. I still remember the smell of the first book my grandfather gave me and the note he wrote inside it. This shows that a paper book can become a treasured memory, not just something to read. You cannot wrap an e-book as a birthday present or keep it on a shelf for your own children.

Admittedly, some people argue that tablets are lighter and can hold hundreds of stories. This is true, and it is useful on long journeys. However, a lighter bag is not worth tired eyes and a wandering mind.
For all these reasons, I am convinced that paper books are still the best way to enjoy a story. Next time you visit the school library, choose a real book. I think you will agree with me.
notes: **Creation 5/5:** all three bullets are covered: opinion (end of paragraph 1), reasons with examples (paragraphs 2–4), what others might say (paragraph 5). The viewpoint is clear and never changes. The friendly, thoughtful tone suits a school magazine.

**Vocabulary 3/3:** precise words (concentrate, notifications, wandering mind, admittedly, convinced) and persuasive tools: rhetorical questions, the rule of three (no notifications, no adverts and no batteries), an emotional anecdote about the grandfather followed by a strong statement (You cannot wrap an e-book…), and direct address (Next time you visit…).

**Structure 7/7:** article title. Introduction with hook (question), background (pupils use tablets) and claim. Three REAP paragraphs, each starting with a clear reason. A short paragraph for the other side. A conclusion that restates the view and ends with an invitation. Linking words guide the reader (One important reason, Another reason, Most importantly, Admittedly, However, For all these reasons).

**Grammar & punctuation 7/7:** complex sentences with when, after and if. Contrast shown with but and however. Question marks used correctly. Commas after opening phrases. A list punctuated correctly. Consistent present tense for the issue and past tense for the memory.
**Spelling 3/3:** ambitious words spelt correctly: especially, headache, concentrate, notification, grandfather, admittedly, convinced.
blocks.marks: Strong answer — Creation 5/5 · Vocabulary 3/3 · Structure 7/7 · Grammar & punctuation 7/7 · Spelling 3/3

blocks.title: Checklist before you finish
items: My opinion is clear in the introduction and again in the conclusion.
The introduction has a hook, background and my opinion.
Each body paragraph follows REAP (Reason, Evidence, Analysis, Persuasive tool).
At least two persuasive tools (rhetorical question, rule of three, emotive words, direct address).
One short paragraph answers what others might say.
Linking words at the start of paragraphs.
The layout matches the format (title for an article, Dear… for a letter).

كل فقرة = سبب واحد بطريقة REAP: السبب، ثم مثال أو دليل، ثم شرح (This shows that…)، ثم أغلق الفقرة بسؤال بلاغي أو جملة قوية.
اذكر رأي المخالفين لك في فقرة قصيرة وردّ عليه (Admittedly… However…). إذا كتبت الجانبين بالتساوي فهذا balanced argument وليس opinion.

items.q: Your head teacher wants to know what pupils think: 'Should every school have a vegetable garden?' Write a letter to the head teacher giving your opinion. (Plan only.)
items.a: Format: Dear Mrs [name], … Yours sincerely, + full name. P1: hook (a fact about how few children know where food comes from) + background + opinion: yes. P2 REAP: pupils learn science outdoors (example: watching seeds grow). P3 REAP: healthier eating (example: pupils are proud to eat what they grow). P4 the other side: it needs time and water. Answer: a garden club can look after it. P5 conclusion: restate the view politely, final thought.

items.q: Decide the text type for each task: (a) 'Explain your view on whether pupils should wear uniforms.' (b) 'Write a speech to persuade your class to join the reading club.' (c) 'Write about the advantages and disadvantages of school trips.'
items.a: (a) Opinion writing: give and explain your view. (b) Persuasive writing: you want people to act (join). (c) Balanced argument: both sides fairly.

items.q: Write a REAP paragraph for the opinion 'Pupils should have longer break times.'
items.a: Example: 'One important reason is that pupils need to move. (R) In our school, break lasts only fifteen minutes, and many pupils spend half of it queueing for food. (E) This means that they return to class restless and unable to concentrate. (A) Is it fair to expect our best work when we have had no time to breathe? (P)'

items.q: Improve this weak opening: 'I am going to write about homework. I think it is good.'
items.a: Example: 'Imagine reaching your exam and realising you had never practised on your own. Homework is sometimes boring, but I strongly believe that it is one of the best ways to prepare for success.' (Hook + background + clear opinion, and no 'I am going to write about'.)

items.q: Rewrite this rude sentence about the other side so that it is polite and still keeps your view: 'People who like screens are wrong and lazy.'
items.a: Example: 'Admittedly, some people prefer screens because they are convenient. However, I believe the benefits of paper books are greater.'

items.q: Which sentence is a better conclusion, and why? (a) 'Also, books are cheap.' (b) 'For all these reasons, I am convinced that reading every day is a habit worth keeping.'
items.a: (b), because it restates the opinion in new words and closes the piece. (a) adds a new reason, which belongs in the body, not in the conclusion.
